concept.name: Bridge
concept.definition: A blockchain bridge is a mechanism that transfers assets, messages or arbitrary data between otherwise isolated blockchain networks, typically by locking or burning assets on the source chain and minting a representation on the destination chain.
concept.intuition: Bridges are ferries between islands that cannot naturally talk to each other — but the ferry company is often the weakest security link in the whole trip.
concept.mechanics: Common designs are lock-and-mint (escrow asset on chain A, mint wrapped asset on chain B), burn-and-mint, and liquidity-network atomic swaps. Trustless bridges rely on the connected chains' own validation (light clients, fraud/validity proofs); trusted bridges introduce external validator sets, multisigs or oracles that users must trust not to collude.
concept.failure_modes: Bridges account for the largest DeFi hacks: smart contract flaws (e.g. the Wormhole exploit), validator collusion in trusted designs, and depegged wrapped assets can all make bridged tokens unbacked; systemic risk compounds because wrapped assets are used as collateral elsewhere.
concept.misconceptions: A wrapped token on another chain is not the same asset — it is an IOU backed by the bridge's custody. 'Trustless' bridges still carry smart contract risk, and native (canonical) L2 bridges are far safer than third-party multisig bridges.
concept.example: To move ETH to Arbitrum via its native bridge, you deposit ETH into the L1 bridge contract and an equivalent amount is credited on L2; using a third-party multisig bridge instead means trusting that a small validator set will not collude to steal the escrow.
